summary.text: A solar flare is a relatively intense, localized emission of electromagnetic radiation in the Sun's atmosphere.
Flares are thought to occur when stored magnetic energy in the Sun's atmosphere accelerates charged particles in the surrounding plasma.
They occur in active regions, often around sunspots, and how often they happen varies with the 11-year solar cycle.

facts.label: Energy source
facts.value: Magnetic energy stored in the corona

facts.label: Radiation range
facts.value: From radio waves to gamma rays

facts.label: Busy times
facts.value: Several per day at solar maximum

items.prompt: A radio operator on the sunlit side of Earth loses short-wave contact while a flare erupts. What is the likely reason?

options.label: Flare radiation raises the ionization of the upper atmosphere
The flare's radiation reaches the ground and overloads the radio
The Sun's glare drowns out the signal at the antenna
Clouds of cooled plasma shade the radio towers

items.explain: Extreme ultraviolet and X-ray radiation is absorbed by the daylight side of the upper atmosphere, which can raise ionization and interfere with short-wave radio.

items.prompt: A flare watcher tallies every flare over a full solar cycle. Which kind will appear most often?

options.label: The most powerful ones, since they build up over time
The weaker ones, because stronger flares are rarer
All strengths in equal numbers
Only the strongest, since weak ones go unseen

items.explain: More powerful flares are less frequent than weaker ones.

items.prompt: A satellite operator wants to know when in the solar cycle flares are most frequent. What should she expect?

options.label: Near solar maximum, with several in a day
Near solar minimum, with several in a day
The same rate throughout the cycle
Only at the very start of each cycle

items.explain: Flare frequency follows the 11-year cycle, ranging from several per day at maxima to fewer than one a week at minima.

items.prompt: Magnetic field lines on the Sun snap together and reconnect in a new arrangement. What does the evidence suggest this does?

options.label: It cools the plasma and slows its particles down
It pulls surface matter down into the core
It releases energy that accelerates charged particles to extreme speeds
It starts the nuclear fusion that powers the Sun

items.explain: Evidence suggests magnetic reconnection leads to the extreme acceleration of charged particles; the sudden release of energy is the origin of the acceleration.

items.prompt: Scientists agree on the source of a flare's energy. What is still unclear?

options.label: Whether flares ever occur on the Sun at all
Whether flares follow the solar cycle
Which layer of the Sun hosts every flare
How the magnetic energy becomes the motion of particles

items.explain: It is not clear how magnetic energy is transformed into the kinetic energy of the particles.

items.prompt: A news story says every solar flare is followed by a giant cloud of ejected material. Is that right?

options.label: Yes; the two are always the same event
No; flares are often, but not always, accompanied by such ejections
No; flares never come with ejections
Yes, but only in the quiet years of the cycle

items.explain: Flares are often, but not always, accompanied by coronal mass ejections and other eruptive phenomena.

paragraphs.heading: A burst of light from the Sun
paragraphs.text: A solar flare is a fairly intense outburst of electromagnetic radiation from one small patch of the Sun's atmosphere. It affects all three layers of that atmosphere: the photosphere, the chromosphere and the corona. The light it gives off covers the whole electromagnetic spectrum, from radio waves at one end to gamma rays at the other. Other stars flare too, and there the event is called a stellar flare.

paragraphs.heading: Where flares break out
paragraphs.text: Flares start in active regions, often near sunspots, where strong magnetic fields push up through the photosphere and tie the corona to the Sun's interior. Many flares come with other eruptions, such as coronal mass ejections and solar particle events, but not all of them do. Flares are also linked to flare sprays, which hurl material outward at 20 to 2,000 kilometres per second.

paragraphs.heading: Where the energy comes from
paragraphs.text: A flare is powered by magnetic energy stored in the corona and let go suddenly, over minutes to tens of minutes. That energy speeds up charged particles, mostly electrons, and their run-ins with the surrounding plasma make the flare shine. The plasma is heated beyond 10⁷ kelvin, while electrons, protons and heavier ions approach the speed of light. The likely trigger is magnetic reconnection: field lines in an arcade, a row of closely spaced coronal loops, quickly rejoin into a lower set of loops. The sudden energy release in that rejoining is what drives the particles.

paragraphs.heading: What is still a puzzle
paragraphs.text: Scientists broadly agree on where a flare's energy comes from, yet the details remain unclear. Nobody yet knows how the magnetic energy turns into the motion of particles. It is also unknown how some particles reach energies of 10⁹ electron volts or more. In some cases the count of accelerated particles even seems larger than the number the coronal loop holds. Predicting flares is still an open research problem.

paragraphs.heading: The life of a flare
paragraphs.text: A flare usually runs through phases: a precursor, then an impulsive phase dominated by particle acceleration, then a gradual phase in which the hot plasma cools. Some flares add a late phase in extreme ultraviolet light that no one can explain yet. After the eruption, loops of hot plasma form across the line dividing opposite magnetic polarities, appearing farther from the source as time passes. In strong flares, typically C-class or above, these loops can merge into a long arch called a post-eruption arcade that may last from hours to days.

paragraphs.heading: How often they happen
paragraphs.text: The number of flares rises and falls with the Sun's 11-year cycle. Near solar maximum there can be several a day; near solar minimum, fewer than one a week. Strong flares are rarer than weak ones: an X10-class flare comes about two or three times per cycle, while M-class flares number about 1,200. In 1984 Erich Rieger and colleagues also found a rhythm of roughly 154 days in gamma-ray flares, now called the Rieger period.

paragraphs.heading: What reaches Earth
paragraphs.text: The extreme ultraviolet and X-ray light from a flare never gets to the ground. The upper atmosphere on Earth's daytime side absorbs it, the ionosphere above all. That can briefly raise the ionosphere's level of ionization, which may disturb short-wave radio.
